Forward-Value Discretization: Faster Stochastic Diffusion Sampling Without High-Order Approximation

Yuchen Jiao ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Email: {yuchenjiao, genli, na.li}@cuhk.edu.hk. Note: The authors contributed equally. Corresponding author: Gen Li.    Na Li11footnotemark: 1 22footnotemark: 2    Changxiao Cai ††thanks: Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA; Email: cxcai@umich.edu.    Yuting Wei ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, USA; Email: ytwei@wharton.upenn.edu.    Gen Li22footnotemark: 2
Abstract

Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality.†† Partial preliminary results of this work appeared in International Conference on Machine Learning 2026 (Jiao et al., 2026). Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.51.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.

Keywords: diffusion model, training-free acceleration, first-order sampler, forward-value discretization, stochastic sampler

1 Introduction

Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have rapidly emerged as a leading paradigm in modern generative modeling, achieving state-of-the-art performance across a wide range applications in generative AI (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020b; Song and Ermon, 2019; Song et al., 2020a; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021). Building on ideas from non-equilibrium thermodynamics (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015), a DPM first defines a forward process that gradually injects noise into the clean data drawn from the true data distribution, and then generates new samples by reversing this process, turning pure noise into high-fidelity outputs. The reversal is driven by a pre-trained neural network that approximate the score functions of the noisy data distributions. DPMs now have shown remarkable success across various domains, including image synthesis (Rombach et al., 2022; Ramesh et al., 2022; Saharia et al., 2022), audio generation (Kong et al., 2021), language models (Li et al., 2022; Sahoo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026), and molecular design (Hoogeboom et al., 2022), underscoring their versatility and impact. See Yang et al. (2023); Croitoru et al. (2023); Lai et al. (2025) for overviews of recent development.

Once a DPM is trained, sampling amounts to discretizing a differential equation that describes the reverse process: either the diffusion SDE (Ho et al., 2020; Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021; Bao et al., 2022) or the diffusion ODE (Song et al., 2020a; Lu et al., 2022b). In practice, a DPM is typically trained as a noise prediction model: given a noisy sample and a time step, it predicts the noise added to the original clean data at that time in the forward process. Since subtracting this noise prediction from the noisy sample yields an estimate of the clean data, the same network equivalently acts as a clean-data predictor. As a result, sample quality relies on two factors: how the diffusion SDE/ODE is discretized, and how the pre-trained DPM is queried along the way.

Diffusion samplers can be broadly classified into two categories, depending on whether noise is injected beyond the initial step. Stochastic samplers (e.g., DDPM (Ho et al., 2020)) add Gaussian noise with during sampling iterations, while deterministic samplers (e.g., DDIM (Song et al., 2020a)) add none beyond initialization. Stochastic samplers tend to produce more diverse samples and give a more natural framework for classifier guidance, which often improves the quality of conditional samples. For example, Figure 1 compares Stable Diffusion samples generated with the prompts (a) “A hand pets a cat in a suitcase” and (b) “A rodeo area with men in cowboy hats, rodeo clowns and an audience in the stands”. For the first prompt, the stochastic samplers SDE-DPMSolver++1 and SDE-DPMSolver++2 (see (17a) and (17b) for their update rules) produce clearly recognizable cats, whereas the deterministic samplers DDIM and DPMSolver-3 (see (32) for the latter’s update rule) primarily depict the suitcase. For the second prompt, the stochastic samplers produce cowboy hats and audience in stands. The corresponding details are less clearly resolved in the deterministic samples. Nevertheless, these benefits come at a price. Empirically, stochastic samplers converge far more slowly than their deterministic counterparts. For instance, On CIFAR-10 with the EDM model, DDPM needs roughly 4040 iterations to achieve lower than 33 in Fréchet inception distance (FID) (Heusel et al., 2017), a metric used to assess the quality of images, whereas DDIM achieves comparable quality in fewer than 1515 iterations. Since each iteration costs one neural function evaluation of the pre-trained DPM and sampling speed is often the primary bottleneck in deployment, this gap has driven growing interest in deterministic samplers.

Higher-order discretization is a widely used training-free approach to accelerating deterministic diffusion sampling (Lu et al., 2022b; Lu et al., 2022a; Zhao et al., 2023). For stochastic samplers, however, increasing the order of a deterministic approximation does not automatically improve the strong convergence order to the underlying diffusion SDE. Strong convergence measures the discrepancy between the numerical and continuous trajectories driven by the same Brownian motion, whereas distributional convergence measures the discrepancy between their laws or between the generated and target distributions. In particular, we show that SDE-DPM-Solver++2 remains first-order convergent despite its higher-order approximation.

This gap motivates the central question of this work:

Can we design a fast stochastic sampler that narrows the performance gap with deterministic samplers?

1.1 Our contributions

We begin by analyzing the convergence rates of existing deterministic and stochastic samplers, including DDIM, DPMSolver(Lu et al., 2022b), and SDE-DPMSolver++(Lu et al., 2022b). For deterministic samplers, prior works have established that a higher-order approximation achieves a corresponding higher-order convergence rate. For instance, DPMSolver-pp converges at a rate of O~​(M−p)\widetilde{O}(M^{-p}), where MM denotes the number of iterations. This work reveals that this correspondence between approximation order and convergence order does not hold for the stochastic SDE-DPM-Solver++ schemes. In particular, SDE-DPM-Solver++2 remains first-order convergent in the strong sense, as established by matching upper and worst-case lower bounds. The reason is that the injected noise makes the generated samples vary too much at each step, for a higher-order expansion to help. This offers one explanation for the practical inefficiency of stochastic samplers.

Next, we explore a simple but under-explored idea: a forward-value discretization of the diffusion ODE. Given the current iterate and time, the idealized forward-value update would evaluate the DPM at the quantities corresponding the next time rather than the current one. We observe that such an update scheme can perform effectively even in the extremely low-NFE regime, which motivates a practical sampler that approximates it. The resulting sampler, named Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), first produces a rough estimate of the next iterate using a vanilla update (e.g., DDIM) with cached model predictions, and then combines the current iterate with a DPM evaluation at this estimate. Critically, it maintains one model evaluation per iteration by reusing the previous evaluation, so its number of model evaluations (NFE) is the same as that of the vanilla sampler. Empirical results show that F-DPMSolver improves FID substantially over higher-order samplers including DPMSolver-2, DPMSolver-3 (Lu et al., 2022a), and UniPC-3 (Zhao et al., 2023), even though its convergence rate still scales as Θ~​(1/M)\widetilde{\Theta}(1/M). These results convey a surprising insight: a first-order sampler can also achieve high practical sampling efficiency.

Inspired by this insight, we extend the forward-value idea to stochastic samplers and propose a fast first-order stochastic sampler, termed Forward DDPM (F-DDPM). Whereas the deterministic sampler evaluates the DPM at a lookahead estimate for the next time step, the stochastic sampler uses an estimate at a carefully chosen cleaner intermediate time to account for subsequent noise injection. To construct this estimate, we form a tailored noise estimate that combines the available noise prediction with the injected noise from the previous step. We also establish a first-order strong error upper bound for F-DDPM. Empirically, F-DDPM consistently improves FID over the evaluated stochastic baselines at the same NFEs and substantially narrows the performance gap with deterministic samplers. With 1.51.5 times as many NFEs, it achieves sample quality comparable to or better than the evaluated deterministic baselines in many tested settings.

1.2 Other related work

Training-free/based acceleration.

Existing acceleration strategies for diffusion sampling can be broadly divided into training-free and training-based approaches. Training-free methods reuse a fixed pre-trained DPM and speed up sampling solely by modifying the sampling update rule, making them broadly applicable to off-the-shelf DPMs. The methods discussed in the introduction belong to this category. In contrast, training-based strategies introduce an additional stage of training (e.g., distillation (Luhman and Luhman, 2021; Salimans and Ho, 2022; Meng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026) and consistency models (Li et al., 2024b; Song et al., 2023)). They aim to shorten sampling trajectories by adapting pre-trained models into related architectures, at the cost of additional training computation. Since our focus is training-free acceleration, we next summarize related work from both practical and theoretical viewpoints.

Training-free acceleration: practice.

Most practical training-free accelerations are driven by higher-order numerical discretizations of the reverse-time SDE/ODE. For ODE-based samplers, a prominent line of work exploits the structure of the diffusion ODE to design higher-order solvers, including DPM-Solver++ (Lu et al., 2022b; Lu et al., 2022a), exponential-integrator-based methods (Zhang and Chen, 2022), and predictor-corrector-based schemes such as UniPC (Zhao et al., 2023). For SDE-based samplers, acceleration is comparatively less explored due to the intrinsic difficulty of SDE discretization, but notable progress includes stochastic Improved Euler’s methods (Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2021), stochastic Adams methods (Xue et al., 2024), and stochastic Runge-Kutta methods (Wu et al., 2024).

Training-free acceleration: theory.

Convergence theory has been established for a wide range of diffusion samplers (Chen et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2024a; Benton et al., 2023; Li and Yan, 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Cai et al., 2026; Jiao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), mostly focusing on standard DDPM and DDIM. For provable acceleration, most existing results likewise concentrate on higher-order discretization and on controlling the resulting discretization error for the reverse-time dynamics (Li and Cai, 2024; Li and Jiao, 2024; Jiao and Li, 2024; Huang et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024a; Yu and Yu, 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Gupta et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). Beyond designing improved solvers, another line of work accelerates generation via parallel sampling that implements multiple denoising steps in parallel (Shih et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2024). In addition to continuous diffusion models, sampling acceleration has also been studied for discrete diffusion models (Li and Cai, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Dmitriev et al., 2026a; Zhao and Cai, 2026; Cai and Li, 2026; Dmitriev et al., 2026b; Chen and Wang, 2026).

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we review the basics of DPM sampling.

2.1 Diffusion processes and parameterization

Forward and reverse processes.

We consider a forward process (𝒙t)0≤t≤T(\bm{x}_{t})_{0\leq t\leq T} in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} whose marginal distribution at time t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] satisfies

𝒙t​=d​αt​𝒙0+σt​𝒛,\bm{x}_{t}\overset{\text{d}}{=}\alpha_{t}\bm{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\bm{z}, (1)

where 𝒙0∼q0\bm{x}_{0}\sim q_{0} is independent of the Gaussian noise 𝒛∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d)\bm{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}_{d}). We denote the distribution of 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t}, or its density, by qtq_{t}. The noise schedules αt\alpha_{t} and σt\sigma_{t} are positive for t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T) and are chosen so that the signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio αt/σt\alpha_{t}/\sigma_{t} decreases strictly with tt and the terminal distribution is approximately Gaussian: qT≈𝒩⁡(0,σ~2​𝑰d)q_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0,\tilde{\sigma}^{2}\bm{I}_{d}).

These forward marginals can be obtained from the SDE

d​𝒙t=f⁡(t)​𝒙t​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​𝝎t,t∈[0,T];𝒙0∼q0,\,\mathrm{d}\bm{x}_{t}=f(t)\bm{x}_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\omega}_{t},\quad t\in[0,T];\qquad\bm{x}_{0}\sim q_{0}, (2)

where (𝝎t)t≥0(\bm{\omega}_{t})_{t\geq 0} denotes a standard dd-dimensional Brownian motion. The coefficients are determined by the noise schedules as follows:

f⁡(t)=d​log⁡αtd​tandg2​(t)=d​σt2d​t−2​σt2​d​log⁡αtd​t.f(t)=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\log\alpha_{t}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\quad\text{and}\quad g^{2}(t)=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{t}^{2}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}-2\sigma_{t}^{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}\log\alpha_{t}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}.

For further details on this formulation, we refer to Kingma et al. (2021).

The time-reversal result of Anderson (1982) gives the reverse SDE associated with (2), which is solved from TT to 00:

d​𝒙t=[f⁡(t)​𝒙t−g2​(t)​𝒔t⋆​(𝒙t)]​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​𝝎~t,t∈[0,T];𝒙T∼qT,\displaystyle\,\mathrm{d}\bm{x}_{t}=\big[f(t)\bm{x}_{t}-g^{2}(t){\bm{s}}_{t}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t})\big]\,\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\,\mathrm{d}\widetilde{\bm{\omega}}_{t},\quad t\in[0,T];\qquad\bm{x}_{T}\sim q_{T}, (3)

where (𝝎~t)t∈[0,T](\widetilde{\bm{\omega}}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} denotes standard Brownian motion running backward from TT to 00, and 𝒔t⋆​(⋅)≔∇log⁡qt​(⋅){\bm{s}}_{t}^{\star}(\cdot)\coloneqq\nabla\log q_{t}(\cdot) is the score of the time-tt marginal. Sampling can alternatively be based on a deterministic process governed by the probability flow ODE:

𝒙˙t=f⁡(t)​𝒙t−12​g2​(t)​𝒔t⋆​(𝒙t),t∈[0,T];𝒙T∼qT.\dot{\bm{x}}_{t}=f(t)\bm{x}_{t}-\frac{1}{2}g^{2}(t){\bm{s}}_{t}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t}),\quad t\in[0,T];\qquad\bm{x}_{T}\sim q_{T}. (4)

At every time tt, both reverse processes have marginal distribution qtq_{t}, matching that of the forward process; see Song et al. (2020b). With the exact score 𝒔t⋆​(⋅){\bm{s}}_{t}^{\star}(\cdot) and initialization from qTq_{T}, both reverse processes recover q0q_{0}. In practice, sampling is approximate because the score is estimated and qTq_{T} is replaced by a Gaussian approximation.

Noise and data prediction.

A noise prediction model 𝜺θ​(𝒙,t)\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t), parameterized by θ\theta, approximates the scaled score function −σt​𝒔t⋆​(𝒙)-\sigma_{t}\bm{s}_{t}^{\star}(\bm{x}). The ideal noise predictor satisfies

𝜺θ⋆​(𝒙,t)=−σt​𝒔t⋆​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[𝒛∣αt​𝒙0+σt​𝒛=𝒙].\displaystyle\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta^{\star}}(\bm{x},t)=-\sigma_{t}\bm{s}_{t}^{\star}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}\big[\bm{z}\mid\alpha_{t}\bm{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\bm{z}=\bm{x}\big]. (5)

For any noise predictor, the corresponding data predictor is defined by

𝝁θ​(𝒙,t)≔𝒙−σt​𝜺θ​(𝒙,t)αt.\displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t)\coloneqq\frac{\bm{x}-\sigma_{t}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t)}{\alpha_{t}}. (6)

In particular, the ideal data predictor satisfies

𝝁θ⋆​(𝒙,t)=𝔼⁡[𝒙0∣αt​𝒙0+σt​𝒛=𝒙].\displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{\theta^{\star}}(\bm{x},t)=\mathbb{E}\big[\bm{x}_{0}\mid\alpha_{t}\bm{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\bm{z}=\bm{x}\big]. (7)

These conditional expectations motivate the names: 𝜺θ\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta} and 𝝁θ\bm{\mu}_{\theta} predict the noise 𝒛\bm{z} and clean data 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0}, respectively, from the noisy input.

We use the time parameterization

whenever it is clear from context.

For numerical sampling, we discretize a truncated interval [tM,t0]⊂(0,T)[t_{M},t_{0}]\subset(0,T) using M+1M+1 time points:

T>t0>t1>⋯>tM−1>tM>0.T>t_{0}>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{M-1}>t_{M}>0. (9)

The corresponding step sizes in the log-SNR variable are

δi≔λti−λti−1>0,i=1,…,M.\delta_{i}\coloneqq\lambda_{t_{i}}-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}>0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,M. (10)

We initialize 𝒙t0∼𝒩⁡(0,σt02​𝑰d)\bm{x}_{t_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{t_{0}}^{2}\bm{I}_{d}), which is a Gaussian approximation to qt0q_{t_{0}}. Both deterministic and stochastic samplers then generate 𝒙t1,…,𝒙tM\bm{x}_{t_{1}},\ldots,\bm{x}_{t_{M}} sequentially to approximate the corresponding diffusion ODE or SDE introduced below.

2.2 Diffusion ODE and deterministic samplers

Diffusion ODE.

Replacing the score function 𝒔t⋆​(𝒙)\bm{s}_{t}^{\star}(\bm{x}) with its approximation −𝜺θ(𝒙,t)/σt-\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t)/\sigma_{t} in the probability flow ODE (4) yields the diffusion ODE:

𝒙˙t=f⁡(t)​𝒙t+g2​(t)2​σt​𝜺θ​(𝒙t,t),t∈[tM,t0].\dot{\bm{x}}_{t}=f(t)\bm{x}_{t}+\frac{g^{2}(t)}{2\sigma_{t}}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t),\qquad t\in[t_{M},t_{0}]. (11)

Under time reparameterization (8), its solution 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} at any time t<st<s can be expressed as

𝒙t\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t} =αtαs​𝒙s−αt​∫λ⁡(s)λ⁡(t)e−λ​𝜺θ​(𝒙t⁡(λ),t⁡(λ))​𝑑λ\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\alpha_{s}}\bm{x}_{s}-\alpha_{t}\int_{\lambda(s)}^{\lambda(t)}{\rm e}^{-\lambda}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}\big(\bm{x}_{t(\lambda)},t(\lambda)\big)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda (12a)
=σtσs​𝒙s+σt​∫λ⁡(s)λ⁡(t)eλ​𝝁θ​(𝒙t⁡(λ),t⁡(λ))​𝑑λ.\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{t}}{\sigma_{s}}\bm{x}_{s}+\sigma_{t}\int_{\lambda(s)}^{\lambda(t)}{\rm e}^{\lambda}\bm{\mu}_{\theta}\big(\bm{x}_{t(\lambda)},t(\lambda)\big)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda. (12b)
Diffusion ODE solvers.

Starting from 𝒙t0\bm{x}_{t_{0}}, an ODE solver produces the states 𝒙t1,…,𝒙tM\bm{x}_{t_{1}},\ldots,\bm{x}_{t_{M}} in sequence, each approximating the continuous solution at the corresponding grid point. The deterministic DDIM sampler (Song et al., 2020a) admits the following first-order update:

𝒙ti\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}} =αtiαti−1​𝒙ti−1−αti​(σti−1αti−1−σtiαti)​𝜺ti−1=αtiαti−1​𝒙ti−1−σti​(eδi−1)​𝜺ti−1.\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}-\alpha_{t_{i}}\bigg(\frac{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}-\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i}}}\bigg)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}=\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}-\sigma_{t_{i}}({\rm e}^{\delta_{i}}-1)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}. (13)

Equivalently, using the data prediction parameterization (6), the DDIM update becomes

𝒙ti=σtiσti−1​𝒙ti−1+σti​(αtiσti−αti−1σti−1)​𝝁ti−1.\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}}=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}+\sigma_{t_{i}}\bigg(\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}-\frac{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\bigg)\bm{\mu}_{t_{i-1}}. (14)

Some popular higher-order multistep solvers approximate the noise predictor along the trajectory by polynomial interpolation of previous model evaluations. For example, DPMSolver-pp uses 𝜺ti−1,…,𝜺ti−p\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}},\ldots,\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-p}} to approximate the integral in (12a) (Lu et al., 2022b). We provide the general update and the commonly used cases p=2,3p=2,3 in Appendix A.1.

2.3 Diffusion SDE and stochastic samplers

Diffusion SDE.

Given a noise predictor 𝜺θ​(𝒙,t)\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t), we can instantiate the SDE (3) by substituting the unknown score function 𝒔t⋆​(𝒙)\bm{s}_{t}^{\star}(\bm{x}) with −𝜺θ(𝒙,t)/σt-\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t)/\sigma_{t}, which yields the diffusion SDE:

d​𝒙t=[f⁡(t)​𝒙t+g2​(t)σt​𝜺θ​(𝒙t,t)]​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​𝝎~t,t∈[tM,t0].\,\mathrm{d}\bm{x}_{t}=\bigg[f(t)\bm{x}_{t}+\frac{g^{2}(t)}{\sigma_{t}}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t},t)\bigg]\,\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\,\mathrm{d}\widetilde{\bm{\omega}}_{t},\qquad t\in[t_{M},t_{0}]. (15)

Under the time reparameterization (8), the solution 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} to the diffusion SDE (15) at any time t<st<s admits the data prediction representation

𝒙t\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t} =σtσs​e−(λt−λs)​𝒙s+2​αt​∫λsλte−2​(λt−λ)​𝝁θ​(𝒙t⁡(λ),t⁡(λ))​𝑑λ+2​σt​∫λsλte−(λt−λ)​d​𝝎¯λ,\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{t}}{\sigma_{s}}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda_{t}-\lambda_{s})}{\bm{x}}_{s}+2\alpha_{t}\int_{\lambda_{s}}^{\lambda_{t}}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda_{t}-\lambda)}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)},t(\lambda))\,\mathrm{d}\lambda+\sqrt{2}\sigma_{t}\int_{\lambda_{s}}^{\lambda_{t}}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda_{t}-\lambda)}\,\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{\lambda}, (16)

Here, 𝝎¯λ\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{\lambda} is a standard dd-dimensional Brownian motion in the increasing variable λ\lambda, obtained by time-changing the reverse-time noise. For a detailed derivation, see Lu et al. (2022a).

Diffusion SDE solvers.

We consider two stochastic samplers based on (16) (Lu et al., 2022a). In both updates, 𝒛1,…,𝒛M\bm{z}_{1},\ldots,\bm{z}_{M} are independent standard Gaussian vectors, independent of the initial state.

    SDE-DPM-Solver++1 (DDPM). The SDE-DPM-Solver++1 can be interpreted as a first-order solver of (16), which admits the following update rule:

    𝒙ti=e−δi​σtiσti−1​𝒙ti−1+αti​(1−e−2​δi)​𝝁θ​(𝒙ti−1,ti−1)+σti​1−e−2​δi​𝒛i.\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}={\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}+\alpha_{t_{i}}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}){\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},t_{i-1})+\sigma_{t_{i}}\sqrt{1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}}\,{\bm{z}}_{i}.     𝒙ti=e−δi​σtiσti−1​𝒙ti−1+αti​(1−e−2​δi)​𝝁θ​(𝒙ti−1,ti−1)+12​δi​αti​(1−e−2​δi)​𝑫ti+σti​1−e−2​δi​𝒛i,\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}={\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}+\alpha_{t_{i}}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}){\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},t_{i-1})+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{i}\alpha_{t_{i}}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}){\bm{D}}_{t_{i}}+\sigma_{t_{i}}\sqrt{1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}}\,{\bm{z}}_{i}, (17b)

    where

    𝑫t1=𝟎,𝑫ti≔𝝁θ​(𝒙ti−1,ti−1)−𝝁θ​(𝒙ti−2,ti−2)λti−1−λti−2,i=2,…,M.{\bm{D}}_{t_{1}}={\bm{0}},\qquad{\bm{D}}_{t_{i}}\coloneqq\frac{{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},t_{i-1})-{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-2}},t_{i-2})}{\lambda_{t_{i-1}}-\lambda_{t_{i-2}}},\quad i=2,\ldots,M.

3 Main results

In this section, we introduce a forward-value stochastic sampler and present the convergence guarantees of both the existing and our proposed stochastic samplers.

3.1 Forward-value discretization

This subsection reviews the forward-value discretization framework and its deterministic implementations from our preliminary conference version (Jiao et al., 2026). This framework provides the basis for the stochastic extension in Section 3.2.

Ideal forward-value discretization.

The DDIM update (14) approximates the data predictor along each integration interval by its value at the current iterate. With few sampling steps, the model evaluation placement can substantially affect sample quality. We therefore consider evaluating the data predictor at the next state-time pair, leading to the ideal forward-value discretization:

𝒙ti𝖿𝗈𝗋\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}}^{\mathsf{for}} =σtiσti−1​𝒙ti−1𝖿𝗈𝗋+(αti−σti​αti−1σti−1)​𝝁θ​(𝒙ti𝖿𝗈𝗋,ti).\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}^{\mathsf{for}}+\left(\alpha_{t_{i}}-\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\right)\bm{\mu}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t_{i}}^{\mathsf{for}},t_{i}). (18)

Here, “forward-value” refers to evaluation at the next endpoint along the sampling direction, even though it is a discretization of the reverse process. Unlike DDIM, this update is implicit because the unknown next state 𝒙ti𝖿𝗈𝗋\bm{x}_{t_{i}}^{\mathsf{for}} also appears in the model input. To obtain an explicit sampler, we replace this input with an estimate of the next state. Under suitable regularity and stability conditions, both DDIM and (18) converge to the same diffusion ODE as the maximum step size vanishes. Our focus is their behavior with few sampling steps.

Figure 2 explores forward-value discretization with few sampling steps. For this experiment, we use five DDIM substeps within each interval (ti−1,ti)(t_{i-1},t_{i}) to obtain an endpoint estimate at tit_{i}, and then use the data prediction at that estimate in the forward-value update. This reference implementation approximates endpoint evaluation without solving the implicit equation (18). It achieves lower FID than DDIM and DPMSolver-2 in the tested settings on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64. Since the endpoint estimates require additional model evaluations, these results motivate the exploration of forward-value evaluation but do not establish an efficiency gain at matched NFE budgets. This raises the practical question: can we approximate forward-value evaluation while retaining one model evaluation per iteration?

F-DPMSolver: first-order forward-value deterministic sampler.

We next describe a practical F-DPMSolver, which replaces the implicit endpoint in (18) with a lookahead estimate. At iteration i=1,…,Mi=1,\ldots,M, we first construct a lookahead estimate 𝒙^ti\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} of the next state using only information available from earlier iterations, without a new model evaluation. We then evaluate the data prediction model at (𝒙^ti,ti)(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},t_{i}) and update the current iterate via

𝒙ti\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}} =σtiσti−1​𝒙ti−1+(αti−σti​αti−1σti−1)​𝝁θ​(𝒙^ti,ti).\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}+\left(\alpha_{t_{i}}-\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\right)\bm{\mu}_{\theta}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},t_{i}). (19)

This update has the same form as DDIM (14), except that the current-state evaluation 𝝁θ​(𝒙ti−1,ti−1)\bm{\mu}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}},t_{i-1}) is replaced with the lookahead evaluation 𝝁θ​(𝒙^ti,ti)\bm{\mu}_{\theta}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},t_{i}).

The data predictor output gives the noise prediction

𝜺~ti≔𝒙^ti−αti​𝝁θ​(𝒙^ti,ti)σti=𝜺θ​(𝒙^ti,ti).\displaystyle\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i}}\coloneqq\frac{\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}-\alpha_{t_{i}}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},t_{i})}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}=\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}},t_{i}). (20)

The noise prediction 𝜺~ti\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i}} is cached for subsequent lookahead steps. We initialize the cache by setting 𝜺~t0=𝒙t0\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{0}}=\bm{x}_{t_{0}} without querying the model. Thus, each iteration requires exactly one new model evaluation, giving a total NFE of MM. Algorithm 3 in Appendix A.3 summarizes the framework.

F-DDIM.

A simple choice of lookahead predictor is the DDIM update formula (13) with the cached noise estimate in place of a fresh model evaluation:

𝒙^ti=αtiαti−1​𝒙ti−1−(αti​σti−1αti−1−σti)​𝜺~ti−1.\displaystyle\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}=\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}-\left(\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}-\sigma_{t_{i}}\right)\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-1}}. (21)

For i≥2i\geq 2, the cached estimate is 𝜺~ti−1=𝜺θ​(𝒙^ti−1,ti−1)\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-1}}=\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}},t_{i-1}). Thus, the predictor starts from the updated state 𝒙ti−1\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}} but reuses the model output computed at the previous lookahead point 𝒙^ti−1\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}. We call this instantiation F-DDIM and give its complete procedure in Algorithm 1.

Higher-order lookahead predictors.

The framework also accommodates predictors that use multiple cached noise estimates to construct the lookahead prediction. We denote the variant based on a pp-th order DPMSolver predictor by F-DPMSolver-pp. At iteration ii, we use a predictor of order ki=min⁡{p,i}k_{i}=\min\{p,i\} with the cached estimates 𝜺~ti−1,…,𝜺~ti−ki\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-1}},\ldots,\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-k_{i}}}. The procedure starts with the F-DDIM predictor and increases the predictor order as more cached outputs become available, without additional model evaluations. For example, the F-DPMSolver-2 predictor uses cached estimates 𝜺~ti−1\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-1}} and 𝜺~ti−2\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-2}} to construct 𝒙^ti\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}} for i≥2i\geq 2. Here, pp specifies the lookahead predictor; it does not imply pp-th order convergence of the resulting sampler.

The deterministic framework shifts model evaluation to a lookahead point while retaining one model evaluation per iteration. Its stochastic extension must additionally account for the noise injected during each update, which affects both the appropriate evaluation time and the construction of the cached noise estimate. We address these two issues in Section 3.2.

3.2 F-DDPM: first-order forward-value stochastic sampler

Building on the forward-value discretization framework, we introduce F-DDPM, a fast stochastic sampler that serves as the forward-value counterpart of DDPM under the data-prediction parametrization in (17a). The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm 2.

At a high level, F-DDPM has the same form as DDPM, and the only difference is where the data prediction model 𝝁θ\bm{\mu}_{\theta} is evaluated. DDPM evaluates it at the current state-time pair (𝒙ti−1,ti−1)(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}},t_{i-1}), whereas F-DDPM evaluates it at a lookahead state-time pair (𝒙^ti′,ti′)(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}^{\prime}},t_{i}^{\prime}) built from information available through step i−1i-1 only. Concretely, for iteration i=1,…,Mi=1,\dots,M, we update the iterate 𝒙ti−1\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}} via

𝒙ti=e−δi​σtiσti−1​𝒙ti−1+αti​(1−e−2​δi)​𝝁θ​(𝒙^ti′,ti′)+σti​1−e−2​δi​𝒛i,\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}={\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}+\alpha_{t_{i}}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}){\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}\big(\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}^{\prime}},t_{i}^{\prime}\big)+\sigma_{t_{i}}\sqrt{1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}}\,{\bm{z}}_{i}, (22)

where 𝒛i​∼𝗂.𝗂.𝖽.​𝒩​(0,𝑰d){\bm{z}}_{i}\overset{\mathsf{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\bm{I}_{d}) for i=1,…,Mi=1,\dots,M are independent Gaussian noise and δi≔λti−λti−1\delta_{i}\coloneqq\lambda_{t_{i}}-\lambda_{t_{i-1}} is defined in (10).

Below, let us specify the evaluation time ti′t_{i}^{\prime} and the lookahead estimate 𝒙^ti′\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}^{\prime}}.

Evaluation time ti′t_{i}^{\prime}.

Recall that for the deterministic sampler F-DPMSolver in (19), the forward-value evaluation is taken at the end time tit_{i} of the current step. In contrast, F-DDPM evaluates the data predictor at a cleaner time ti′<tit_{i}^{\prime}<t_{i}, chosen to account for the noise injected during the stochastic update.

For each i≥1i\geq 1, let ti′t_{i}^{\prime} be the time whose log-SNR λti′\lambda_{t_{i}^{\prime}} exceeds that of the end time tit_{i} by δi>0\delta_{i}>0:

λti′=λti+δi=λti−1+2​δi.\displaystyle\lambda_{t_{i}^{\prime}}=\lambda_{t_{i}}+\delta_{i}=\lambda_{t_{i-1}}+2\delta_{i}. (23)

Since λt\lambda_{t} is decreasing in tt, the evaluation time ti′<tit_{i}^{\prime}<t_{i} lies past the current end time tit_{i} along the sampling direction. When the time grid is uniform in log-SNR, we have ti′=ti+1t_{i}^{\prime}=t_{i+1} for i=1,…,M−1i=1,\ldots,M-1.

To motivate this choice, denote by 𝒙t⋆{\bm{x}}_{t}^{\star} the solution to the SDE (2) for the forward process. Conditioned on the state 𝒙ti−1⋆\bm{x}^{\star}_{t_{i-1}} at time ti−1t_{i-1} and the clean data 𝒙0⋆\bm{x}^{\star}_{0}, the posterior distribution of the state 𝒙ti⋆\bm{x}^{\star}_{t_{i}} at time tit_{i} is Gaussian with covariance σti2​(1−e−2​δi)​𝑰d\sigma_{t_{i}}^{2}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}})\bm{I}_{d} and mean

where 𝜺=(𝒙ti−1⋆−αti−1​𝒙0⋆)/σti−1∼𝒩⁡(0,𝑰d)\bm{\varepsilon}={({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}^{\star}-\alpha_{t_{i-1}}{\bm{x}}_{0}^{\star})}/{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\bm{I}_{d}) is independent of 𝒙0⋆{\bm{x}}_{0}^{\star}. =αti−1αti−1′​(αti−1′​𝝁θ​(𝒙ti−1′,ti−1′)+σti−1′​𝜺θ​(𝒙ti−1′,ti−1′))+σti−1​1−e−2​δi−1​𝒛i−1\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}^{\prime}}}\Big(\alpha_{t_{i-1}^{\prime}}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}^{\prime}},t_{i-1}^{\prime})+\sigma_{t_{i-1}^{\prime}}{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}^{\prime}},t_{i-1}^{\prime})\Big)+\sigma_{t_{i-1}}\sqrt{1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i-1}}}{\bm{z}}_{i-1}

To conclude, each iteration of F-DDPM requires only one new model evaluation, at (𝒙^ti′,ti′)(\widehat{{\bm{x}}}_{t_{i}^{\prime}},t_{i}^{\prime})—the resulting noise prediction is used both to compute the data prediction in (22) and to form the noise estimate for the next iteration. Thus, F-DDPM uses MM model evaluations in total.

3.3 Convergence analysis

We analyze the trajectory discretization errors of the forward-value samplers and the baseline diffusion ODE and SDE solvers. The numerical sampler and its continuous reference process use the same initial state. In the stochastic setting, they are additionally coupled through the same Brownian motion. These convergence guarantees characterize approximation to the continuous dynamics and complement the few-step sample-quality comparisons in Section 4.

Convergence criteria.

We consider time grids {ti}i=0M\{t_{i}\}_{i=0}^{M} with fixed endpoints t0t_{0} and tMt_{M}, corresponding to a fixed finite log-SNR interval. Convergence rates are measured as M→∞M\to\infty. For deterministic samplers, we fix the initial state 𝒙t0\bm{x}_{t_{0}} and measure the Euclidean error at the final time.

Definition 1.

A deterministic diffusion sampler has convergence order at least kk if

‖𝒙tM−𝒙tM⋆‖2=O⁡(1/Mk),\displaystyle\big\|\bm{x}_{t_{M}}-\bm{x}_{t_{M}}^{\star}\big\|_{2}=O(1/M^{k}),

where 𝒙t⋆\bm{x}_{t}^{\star} is the exact solution to the diffusion ODE (12a) when initialized at 𝒙t0⋆=𝒙t0{\bm{x}}_{t_{0}}^{\star}={\bm{x}}_{t_{0}}. In particular, for 0≤t≤t00\leq t\leq t_{0}, it satisfies

𝒙t⋆=αtαt0​𝒙t0⋆−αt​∫λt0λte−λ​𝜺θ​(𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆,t⁡(λ))​𝑑λ,0≤t≤t0.\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t}^{\star}=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\alpha_{t_{0}}}\bm{x}_{t_{0}}^{\star}-\alpha_{t}\int_{\lambda_{t_{0}}}^{\lambda_{t}}{\rm e}^{-\lambda}\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}\big(\bm{x}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star},t(\lambda)\big)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda,\qquad 0\leq t\leq t_{0}. (28)

For stochastic samplers, we measure the expected Euclidean error under a common initialization and Brownian motion.

Definition 2.

A stochastic diffusion sampler has convergence order at least kk if

𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tM−𝒙tM⋆‖2]=O⁡(1/Mk),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}^{\star}\big\|_{2}\Big]=O(1/M^{k}),

where 𝒙t⋆{\bm{x}}_{t}^{\star} is the exact solution to the diffusion SDE (16), initialized at 𝒙t0⋆=𝒙t0\bm{x}_{t_{0}}^{\star}=\bm{x}_{t_{0}} and driven by the same Brownian 𝝎¯λ\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{\lambda} as the numerical sampler. In particular, for 0≤t<s≤t00\leq t<s\leq t_{0}, it satisfies

𝒙t⋆=σtσs​e−(λt−λs)​𝒙s⋆+2​αt​∫λsλte−2​(λt−λ)​𝝁θ​(𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆,λ)​𝑑λ+2​σt​∫λsλte−(λt−λ)​d​𝝎¯λ.\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t}^{\star}=\frac{\sigma_{t}}{\sigma_{s}}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda_{t}-\lambda_{s})}{\bm{x}}_{s}^{\star}+2\alpha_{t}\int_{\lambda_{s}}^{\lambda_{t}}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda_{t}-\lambda)}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star},\lambda)\mathrm{d}\lambda+\sqrt{2}\sigma_{t}\int_{\lambda_{s}}^{\lambda_{t}}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda_{t}-\lambda)}\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{\lambda}. (29)

The Gaussian vectors 𝒛i\bm{z}_{i} in the stochastic updates are coupled to this Brownian motion through

σti​1−e−2​δi​𝒛i=2​σti​∫λti−1λtie−(λti−λ)​d​𝝎¯λ.\sigma_{t_{i}}\sqrt{1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}}{\bm{z}}_{i}=\sqrt{2}\sigma_{t_{i}}\int_{\lambda_{t_{i-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{i}}}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda_{t_{i}}-\lambda)}\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{\lambda}.
Regularity assumptions.

We impose conditions on the sampling grids, noise schedules, and prediction model to control the discretization errors. The model assumptions are stated in terms of the data predictor 𝝁θ\bm{\mu}_{\theta} in (6), which has one-to-one correspondence with the noise predictor 𝜺θ\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}.

Assumption 1.

We assume that the time grid satisfies maxi∈[M]⁡δi=O⁡(1/M)\max_{i\in[M]}\delta_{i}={O}(1/M) and maxi∈[M]⁡δi/mini∈[M]⁡δi=O⁡(1)\max_{i\in[M]}\delta_{i}/\min_{i\in[M]}\delta_{i}=O(1). The noise schedules αt⁡(λ)\alpha_{t(\lambda)} and σt⁡(λ)\sigma_{t(\lambda)} are positive and twice continuously differentiable on [λt0,max1≤m≤M⁡λtm′][\lambda_{t_{0}},\max_{1\leq m\leq M}\lambda_{t_{m}^{\prime}}], with αt⁡(λ)\alpha_{t(\lambda)} nondecreasing and σt⁡(λ)\sigma_{t(\lambda)} nonincreasing as functions of λ\lambda. In addition, for every 𝒙∈ℝd\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and λ∈[λt0,max1≤m≤M⁡λtm′]\lambda\in[\lambda_{t_{0}},\max_{1\leq m\leq M}\lambda_{t_{m}^{\prime}}], we assume that the data predictor 𝝁θ​(𝒙,t)\bm{\mu}_{\theta}(\bm{x},t) satisfies

  1. (A1)

    ‖𝝁θ​(𝒙,t)‖≤Lμ\|{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}},t)\|\leq L_{\mu};

  2. (A2)

    ‖∇𝒙𝝁θ​(𝒙,t)‖≤Lx/αt\|\nabla_{\bm{x}}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}},t)\|\leq L_{x}/\alpha_{t};

  3. (A3)

    ‖∇𝒙2​𝝁θ​(𝒙,t)‖≤Hx\|\nabla_{\bm{x}}^{2}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}},t)\|\leq H_{x};

  4. (A4)

    ‖∂∂λ​𝝁θ​(𝒙,t⁡(λ))‖≤Lt\big\|\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}\big({\bm{x}},t(\lambda)\big)\big\|\leq L_{t};

  5. (A5)

    ‖∂2∂λ2​𝝁θ​(𝒙,t⁡(λ))‖≤Ht\big\|\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{2}}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}\big({\bm{x}},t(\lambda)\big)\big\|\leq H_{t};

  6. (A6)

    ‖∂∂λ​∇𝒙𝝁θ​(𝒙,t⁡(λ))‖≤H\big\|\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\nabla_{\bm{x}}{\bm{\mu}}_{\theta}\big({\bm{x}},t(\lambda)\big)\big\|\leq H.

Assumption 1 imposes a maximum log-SNR step size of O⁡(M−1)O(M^{-1}), a bounded ratio between the largest and smallest steps, monotonicity and smoothness of the noise schedules, and boundedness and regularity of the data predictor. The maximum-step condition and spatial Lipschitz regularity have been assumed in diffusion solver analyses (Lu et al., 2022b; Zhao et al., 2023). The bounded step ratio simplifies the treatment of nonuniform grids, and is mainly used for the analysis of SDE-DPMSolver++2. The derivative conditions support the Taylor expansions and remainder estimates used in our proofs. Related total-derivative assumptions along ODE trajectories appear in DPM-Solver and UniPC (Lu et al., 2022b; Zhao et al., 2023), while stochastic solver analyses also impose spatial and temporal coefficient regularity (Gonzalez et al., 2023).

3.3.1 Convergence characterization of deterministic samplers

Previous analyses establish error upper bounds for deterministic diffusion solvers; see, for example, (Lu et al., 2022b, Theorem 3.2) and (Zheng et al., 2023, Theorem 3.3). We complement these guarantees with matching worst-case lower bounds for DDIM and DPMSolver-2. Notably, these lower bounds cannot be avoided even in the most ideal setting when the true score functions are accessible (i.e., there is no score matching error).

Theorem 1.

Under Assumption 1, the following convergence guarantees hold:

  • •

    DDIM (13) converges with order 11 (in terms of Definition 1);

  • •

    The DPMSolver-2 (cf. (31)) converges with order 22.

In addition, for any time grid {ti}i=0M\{t_{i}\}_{i=0}^{M} satisfying δi=λti−λti−1=O⁡(M−1)\delta_{i}=\lambda_{t_{i}}-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}=O(M^{-1}), the following bounds hold, each for some target distribution:

  • •

    Deterministic DDIM has convergence order at most 11;

  • •

    DPMSolver-2 (cf. (31)) has convergence order at most 22.

Theorem 1 shows that the error upper bounds for DDIM and DPMSolver-2 are sharp. For these deterministic methods, the higher-order approximation improves the convergence order from 11 to 22. The proof is deferred to Appendix B.

3.3.2 Convergence characterization of stochastic samplers

We next analyze SDE-DPMSolver++1 and SDE-DPMSolver++2. Theorem 2 gives first-order error upper bounds for both methods under the expected Euclidean error in Definition 2.

Theorem 2.

Under Assumption 1, both SDE-DPMSolver++1 and SDE-DPMSolver++2 satisfy the first-order error bound in Definition 2.

The proof is deferred to Appendix C. We establish matching worst-case lower bounds next. These bounds hold even with exact score functions, showing that the first-order rates cannot generally be improved for these methods.

Theorem 3.

Consider any time grid {ti}i=0M\{t_{i}\}_{i=0}^{M} satisfying

δi=λti−λti−1=O⁡(M−1),andmaxi⁡δimini⁡δi=O⁡(1).\delta_{i}=\lambda_{t_{i}}-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}=O({M}^{-1}),\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\max_{i}\delta_{i}}{\min_{i}\delta_{i}}=O(1).

For each of SDE-DPMSolver++1 and SDE-DPMSolver++2, there exists a target distribution for which its convergence order is at most 11.

The proof of this result is postponed to Appendix D. Together, Theorems 2 and 3 establish sharp first-order convergence rates for both methods. In particular, the higher-order approximation used by SDE-DPMSolver++2 does not improve its strong convergence order over SDE-DPMSolver++1. Thus, increasing the order of a deterministic approximation does not automatically improve the strong convergence order of the resulting stochastic sampler.

3.3.3 Convergence of forward-value samplers

We now analyze the forward-value samplers introduced in Sections 3.1 and 3.2. We first establish a first-order error upper bound for F-DDIM and show that this rate is sharp in the worst case.

Theorem 4.

Under Assumption 1, F-DDIM satisfies the first-order error bound in Definition 1. Moreover, for any time grids {λti}i=0M\{\lambda_{t_{i}}\}_{i=0}^{M} satisfying δi=O⁡(M−1)\delta_{i}=O(M^{-1}), there exists a target distribution for which the convergence order of F-DDIM is at most 11.

The proof is postponed to Appendix E. Higher-order discretization is a common approach to improving diffusion sampling with few steps. Theorem 4, together with the experiments in Section 4.1, shows that good few-step sample quality can also be achieved by a first-order sampler: F-DDIM remains first-order convergent while attaining competitive or better FID than higher-order baselines at small NFE budgets. This highlights model evaluation placement as a design principle that complements improvements in convergence order. The distinction is particularly relevant to stochastic sampling, where the higher-order approximation in SDE-DPMSolver++2 does not improve its first-order strong convergence rate. These observations explain the forward-value design of F-DDPM in Section 3.2, which applies this principle while accounting for the injected noise.

For completeness, we also establish a first-order error upper bound for F-DDPM.

Theorem 5.

Under Assumption 1, F-DDPM satisfies the first-order error bound in Definition 2.

The detailed proof of this result is postponed to Appendix F. This guarantee complements the empirical results in Section 4 tells that: F-DDPM improves sample quality at small NFE budgets while retaining a first-order strong convergence guarantee.

4 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the forward-value samplers from two perspectives. First, we examine whether the first-order deterministic sampler F-DDIM achieves competitive sample quality at small NFEs. Second, we compare F-DDPM with stochastic baselines at matched NFEs and with deterministic samplers using 1.51.5 times their NFEs.

Models and datasets.

We evaluate the samplers on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN, and FFHQ datasets. For CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009), we use unconditional and class-conditional EDM models (Karras et al., 2022). For ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), we use EDM2-S and EDM2-L at resolution 64×6464\times 64, and EDM2-XS and EDM2-XXL at resolution 512×512512\times 512. For LSUN bedrooms (Yu et al., 2015) and FFHQ (Karras et al., 2019), we use pre-trained latent diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2022; Blattmann et al., 2022) with noise predictors.

Evaluation settings.

We measure sample quality using FID computed from 50K generated samples, with lower scores indicating better quality. In the FID tables, bold indicates the lowest FID in each row. Computational budgets are reported as the number of neural function evaluations (NFE). For LSUN and FFHQ, we compute the reference statistics ourselves; the resulting FID scores may therefore differ from those reported in other studies. The reference statistics and the code used to generate them are available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DPMSolver.

For EDM and EDM2, we directly construct the sampling noise levels using their native ρ\rho-parameterized schedule. For the latent diffusion models considered here, the noise predictor is trained at discrete noise levels specified by a reference schedule {(αj𝗋𝖾𝖿,σj𝗋𝖾𝖿)}j=0M𝗋𝖾𝖿\{(\alpha_{j}^{\mathsf{ref}},\sigma_{j}^{\mathsf{ref}})\}_{j=0}^{M^{\mathsf{ref}}}. To perform sampling with MM iterations, we select M+1M+1 levels from this schedule according to

ri\displaystyle r_{i} =𝗋𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽⁡(i​M𝗋𝖾𝖿M),\displaystyle=\mathsf{round}\left(\frac{iM^{\mathsf{ref}}}{M}\right),
αti\displaystyle\alpha_{t_{i}} =αri𝗋𝖾𝖿,σti=σri𝗋𝖾𝖿,i=0,…,M.\displaystyle=\alpha_{r_{i}}^{\mathsf{ref}},\qquad\sigma_{t_{i}}=\sigma_{r_{i}}^{\mathsf{ref}},\qquad i=0,\ldots,M.

4.1 Evaluation of F-DDIM

We first evaluate whether F-DDIM, as a first-order sampler, can achieve good few-step sample quality.

Experimental setup.

We compare F-DDIM with deterministic DDIM, a second-order DPM Solver (DPMSolver-2, see (31)), a third-order DPM Solver (DPMSolver-3, see (32)), and a third-order predictor-corrector-based sampler (UniPC-3, see (33b) and (33a)). All methods are evaluated at NFE budgets in {4,5,6,8,10}\{4,5,6,8,10\}. The baseline update formulas are given in Appendix A.1.

Quantitative results (FID).

Tables 1 and 2, together with Tables 7 and 8 in Appendix A, report the FID results. F-DDIM substantially improves upon DDIM across the tested settings. On ImageNet-64 and ImageNet-512, it achieves the lowest FID among the compared methods at all tested NFEs and model sizes reported in Tables 2 and 7. On unconditional CIFAR-10, F-DDIM achieves the lowest FID at NFE budgets 44, 55, 66, and 88. On conditional CIFAR-10, it achieves the lowest FID at budgets 44, 55, and 66, while UniPC-3 performs better at budgets 88 and 1010. These results demonstrate that F-DDIM, as a first-order sampler, can achieve competitive few-step sample quality relative to higher-order deterministic baselines.

Additional results, including generated samples, runtime comparisons, larger NFE budgets, and higher-order lookahead predictors, are provided in Appendix A.

4.2 Evaluation of F-DDPM

Experimental setup.

We compare F-DDPM with SDE-DPMSolver++1 (17a) and SDE-DPMSolver++2 (17b) at NFEs in {6,9,12,15}\{6,9,12,15\}. We also compare these stochastic samplers with DDIM, DPMSolver-3, and F-DDIM at NFEs in {4,6,8,10}\{4,6,8,10\}, respectively. Thus, each stochastic sampler uses 1.51.5 times the NFE of the deterministic methods in the corresponding table row. The noise schedules follow the subsampling procedure described above.

For the latent diffusion models considered here, model evaluations are restricted to supported reference noise levels. At iteration ii, we select the noise level whose signal-to-noise ratio is closest to that of the lookahead time ti′t_{i}^{\prime}:

ji⋆\displaystyle j_{i}^{\star} ∈arg​minj∈𝒥i𝗋𝖾𝖿⁡|αti′σti′−αj𝗋𝖾𝖿σj𝗋𝖾𝖿|,\displaystyle\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{\mathsf{ref}}}\left|\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}^{\prime}}}{\sigma_{t_{i}^{\prime}}}-\frac{\alpha_{j}^{\mathsf{ref}}}{\sigma_{j}^{\mathsf{ref}}}\right|,

where

𝒥i𝗋𝖾𝖿={0≤j≤M𝗋𝖾𝖿:αj𝗋𝖾𝖿σj𝗋𝖾𝖿≥αtiσti}.\mathcal{J}_{i}^{\mathsf{ref}}=\Big\{0\leq j\leq M^{\mathsf{ref}}:\frac{\alpha_{j}^{\mathsf{ref}}}{\sigma_{j}^{\mathsf{ref}}}\geq\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i}}}\Big\}.

The selected reference noise level is used for both the model evaluation and the corresponding F-DDPM update coefficients.

Comparison with stochastic baselines.

Tables 3–6 compare the stochastic samplers across various NFEs. F-DDPM achieves the lowest FID among the three stochastic methods in every tested setting. For example, on unconditional CIFAR-10 with 99 model evaluations, F-DDPM achieves an FID of 8.638.63, compared with 55.5255.52 for SDE-DPMSolver++1 and 17.8917.89 for SDE-DPMSolver++2. These improvements are consistent across datasets, model sizes, conditional and unconditional settings, and pixel-space and latent-space generation.

Comparison with deterministic baselines.

The same tables compare the stochastic samplers using 1.5​B1.5B model evaluations with deterministic samplers using BB evaluations, where B∈{4,6,8,10}B\in\{4,6,8,10\}. Under this budget allocation, F-DDPM achieves lower FID than all three deterministic baselines on unconditional CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-512. It also outperforms all three on conditional CIFAR-10 at B=4,6,8B=4,6,8 and on LSUN at B=6,8,10B=6,8,10. Deterministic samplers retain an advantage on ImageNet-64 and in several FFHQ settings. Overall, these comparisons show that F-DDPM narrows the empirical sampling-efficiency gap with deterministic methods, while still using a larger NFE budget.

Qualitative comparisons.

Figures 3 and 4 show representative samples on ImageNet-64 and FFHQ. Additional examples on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-512, and LSUN are provided in Figures 13, 14, 15, and 16 in the appendix. Within each comparison, the stochastic samplers use the same initial noise and Brownian motion. At small NFEs, F-DDPM often produces clearer structures and finer visual details than the stochastic baselines, consistent with the FID comparisons. For example, the ImageNet-64 samples show more distinct object boundaries and background details.

5 Discussion

We studied forward-value discretization as a training-free approach for accelerating diffusion sampling. Our analysis establishes first-order strong error bounds and matching worst-case lower bounds for SDE-DPMSolver++1 and SDE-DPMSolver++2. Thus, the higher-order approximation in SDE-DPMSolver++2 does not improve its strong convergence order. Together with the first-order characterization of F-DDIM and its competitive few-step sample quality, these results highlight model evaluation placement as a design principle that complements increasing the convergence order.

Building on the deterministic forward-value framework, we developed F-DDPM by accounting for noise injection in the choice of evaluation time and the construction of the lookahead estimate. The method requires one model evaluation per iteration and admits a first-order strong convergence guarantee. Across the tested settings, F-DDPM achieves lower FID than the stochastic baselines at the same NFE budgets. With 1.51.5 times the NFE of the deterministic baselines, it also achieves competitive sample quality in many settings, although deterministic methods retain an advantage in others. These results demonstrate the practical potential of forward-value evaluation for reducing the efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling.

Several questions remain open. First, the convergence guarantees do not explain why changing evaluation placement improves few-step sample quality. Second, the behavior of the method under classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance deserves further study, where guidance strength can amplify errors and alter the effective dynamics. Finally, applications to inverse problems, such as deblurring and super-resolution, require further investigation of how forward-value updates interact with measurement consistency constraints.

Appendix A Additional sampler details and experimental results

A.1 Baseline deterministic samplers

We describe the deterministic baseline samplers used in Section 4.1.

Multistep DPMSolver updates.

For the noise-prediction-based multistep solvers, we write 𝜺tj=𝜺θ​(𝒙tj,tj)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{j}}=\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t_{j}},t_{j}). To construct a pp-th order update, we approximate the noise predictor along the trajectory by a polynomial of degree at most p−1p-1, interpolating the previous pp model evaluations. Integrating this polynomial in (12a) gives (Lu et al., 2022b)

𝒙ti\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}} =𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋​p​(𝒙ti−1,𝜺ti−1,⋯,𝜺ti−p)\displaystyle=\mathsf{ODESolver}p(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}},\cdots,\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-p}})
≔αtiαti−1​𝒙ti−1−αti​e−λti−1​∑k=0p−1φk​(δi)k!​𝒚k+1,i≥p,\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}-\alpha_{t_{i}}{\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}}\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\varphi_{k}(\delta_{i})}{k!}{\bm{y}}_{k+1},\quad i\geq p, (30)

where scalar functions φk\varphi_{k} are defined by

φ0​(x)\displaystyle\varphi_{0}(x) =1−e−x,\displaystyle=1-{\rm e}^{-x},
φk​(x)\displaystyle\varphi_{k}(x) =∫0xe−λλkdλ=kφk−1(x)−xke−x,k=1,⋯,p−1,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{x}{\rm e}^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda=k\varphi_{k-1}(x)-x^{k}{\rm e}^{-x},\quad k=1,\cdots,p-1,

The vectors 𝒚k+1\bm{y}_{k+1} define the interpolating polynomial

Pi​(λ)=∑k=0p−1(λ−λti−1)kk!​𝒚k+1,P_{i}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{(\lambda-\lambda_{t_{i-1}})^{k}}{k!}\bm{y}_{k+1},

which satisfies Pi​(λti−j)=𝜺ti−jP_{i}(\lambda_{t_{i-j}})=\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-j}} for j=1,…,pj=1,\ldots,p. Equivalently, the matrix 𝒀=[𝒚1,…,𝒚p]⊤∈ℝp×d\bm{Y}=[\bm{y}_{1},\ldots,\bm{y}_{p}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} solves

𝑨𝒀=𝑩,𝑨=[(λti−j−λti−1)k−1(k−1)!]1≤j,k≤p∈ℝp×p,and𝑩=[𝜺ti−j⊤]1≤j≤p∈ℝp×d.{\bm{A}}{\bm{Y}}={\bm{B}},\quad{\bm{A}}=\left[\frac{(\lambda_{t_{i-j}}-\lambda_{t_{i-1}})^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}\right]_{1\leq j,k\leq p}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p},\quad\mathrm{and}\quad{\bm{B}}=[\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-j}}^{\top}]_{1\leq j\leq p}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d}.

The cases p=2p=2 and p=3p=3 give the following DPMSolver-2 and DPMSolver-3 updates.

  • •

    DPMSolver-2. The first state 𝒙t1\bm{x}_{t_{1}} is initialized using one DDIM step (13). For i=2,…,Mi=2,\ldots,M, the update is

    𝒙ti\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}} =𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟤⁡(𝒙ti−1,𝜺ti−1,𝜺ti−2)\displaystyle=\mathsf{ODESolver2}(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}})
    ≔αtiαti−1​𝒙ti−1+αti​[(e−λti−e−λti−1)​𝜺ti−1+ϕ1,i​𝑫ti],\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}+\alpha_{t_{i}}\Big[\big({\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i}}}-{\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}}\big)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}+\phi_{1,i}\bm{D}_{t_{i}}\Big], (31a)
    where
    𝑫ti\displaystyle\bm{D}_{t_{i}} ≔𝜺ti−1−𝜺ti−2δi−1,ϕ1,i≔(δi+1)​e−λti−e−λti−1,i≥2.\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}-\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}}}{\delta_{i-1}},\qquad\phi_{1,i}\coloneqq(\delta_{i}+1){\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i}}}-{\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}},\qquad i\geq 2. (31b)
  • •

    DPMSolver-3. The first state 𝒙t1\bm{x}_{t_{1}} is initialized using one DDIM step (13), and the second state 𝒙t2\bm{x}_{t_{2}} is computed using DPMSolver-2 (31) with 𝜺t0\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{0}} and 𝜺t1\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{1}}. Once three previous model evaluations are available, the update for i=3,…,Mi=3,\ldots,M is

    𝒙ti\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}} =𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟥⁡(𝒙ti−1,𝜺ti−1,𝜺ti−2,𝜺ti−3)\displaystyle=\mathsf{ODESolver3}(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-3}})
    ≔αtiαti−1𝒙ti−1+αti[(e−λti−e−λti−1)𝜺ti−1\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\alpha_{t_{i}}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}+\alpha_{t_{i}}\Bigg[\big({\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i}}}-{\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i-1}}}\big)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}
    +ϕ1,i(λti−1−λti−3)​𝑫1,ti−(λti−1−λti−2)​𝑫2,tiλti−2−λti−3+ϕ2,i𝑫1,ti−𝑫2,tiλti−2−λti−3],\displaystyle\hskip 90.00014pt+\phi_{1,i}\frac{(\lambda_{t_{i-1}}-\lambda_{t_{i-3}})\bm{D}_{1,t_{i}}-(\lambda_{t_{i-1}}-\lambda_{t_{i-2}})\bm{D}_{2,t_{i}}}{\lambda_{t_{i-2}}-\lambda_{t_{i-3}}}+\phi_{2,i}\frac{\bm{D}_{1,t_{i}}-\bm{D}_{2,t_{i}}}{\lambda_{t_{i-2}}-\lambda_{t_{i-3}}}\Bigg], (32a)
    where ϕ1,i\phi_{1,i} is defined in (31b), and
    𝑫1,ti\displaystyle\bm{D}_{1,t_{i}} ≔𝜺ti−1−𝜺ti−2λti−1−λti−2,𝑫2,ti≔𝜺ti−1−𝜺ti−3λti−1−λti−3,ϕ2,i≔δi2​e−λti+2​ϕ1,i,i≥3.\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}-\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}}}{\lambda_{t_{i-1}}-\lambda_{t_{i-2}}},\qquad\bm{D}_{2,t_{i}}\coloneqq\frac{\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}}-\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-3}}}{\lambda_{t_{i-1}}-\lambda_{t_{i-3}}},\qquad\phi_{2,i}\coloneqq\delta_{i}^{2}{\rm e}^{-\lambda_{t_{i}}}+2\phi_{1,i},\qquad i\geq 3. (32b)
UniPC-3.

UniPC-3 combines a predictor with a corrector (Zhao et al., 2023). Let 𝒙ti\bm{x}_{t_{i}} denote the predicted state and 𝒙ti𝖼𝗈𝗋\bm{x}_{t_{i}}^{\mathsf{cor}} the corrected state. The model is evaluated at the predicted state, 𝜺ti=𝜺θ​(𝒙ti,ti)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i}}=\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t_{i}},t_{i}). The corrected initialization is 𝒙t0𝖼𝗈𝗋=𝒙t0\bm{x}_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{cor}}=\bm{x}_{t_{0}}. In the first step, 𝒙t1\bm{x}_{t_{1}} is computed using one DDIM step (13) from 𝒙t0{\bm{x}}_{t_{0}}, and 𝒙t1𝖼𝗈𝗋\bm{x}_{t_{1}}^{\mathsf{cor}} is computed using DPMSolver-2 (31) with 𝜺t0\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{0}} and 𝜺t1\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{1}}. For i≥2i\geq 2, the corrected state 𝒙ti−1𝖼𝗈𝗋\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}^{\mathsf{cor}} is used to compute the next predicted state 𝒙ti\bm{x}_{t_{i}} using DPMSolver-2 (31) with 𝜺ti−1\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}} and 𝜺ti−2\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}}.

𝒙ti\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}} =𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟤⁡(𝒙ti−1𝖼𝗈𝗋,𝜺ti−1,𝜺ti−2),\displaystyle=\mathsf{ODESolver2}(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}^{\mathsf{cor}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}}), (33a)
where 𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟤\mathsf{ODESolver2} is given in (31). We then evaluate 𝜺ti=𝜺θ​(𝒙ti,ti)\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i}}=\bm{\varepsilon}_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t_{i}},t_{i}) and use this output to correct the current interval:
𝒙ti𝖼𝗈𝗋\displaystyle\bm{x}_{t_{i}}^{\mathsf{cor}} =𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟥⁡(𝒙ti−1𝖼𝗈𝗋,𝜺ti,𝜺ti−1,𝜺ti−2),\displaystyle=\mathsf{ODESolver3}(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}}^{\mathsf{cor}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-1}},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t_{i-2}}), (33b)
where 𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟥\mathsf{ODESolver3} is defined in (32).

At the final step, we return the predicted state 𝒙tM\bm{x}_{t_{M}} without evaluating the model at tMt_{M} or applying the corrector. Including the initial model evaluation at t0t_{0}, the total NFE is MM.

A.2 Additional results for F-DDIM

Quantitative results (FID).

Tables 7 and 8 supplement the results in Section 4.1. On ImageNet-64, F-DDIM achieves the lowest FID among the compared methods across all tested NFEs and model sizes. On FFHQ, it achieves the lowest FID at all tested NFEs except NFE=4=4, where DPMSolver-3 performs slightly better. On LSUN bedrooms, F-DDIM performs best at NFE =5,6=5,6, while DPMSolver-3 performs best at NFE =4=4 and DPMSolver-2 at NFE =8,10=8,10. Across these settings, F-DDIM consistently improves upon DDIM and remains competitive with higher-order methods.

Qualitative comparisons.

Figures 5–10 show additional samples on ImageNet-64, ImageNet-512, FFHQ, LSUN bedrooms, and CIFAR-10. The comparisons cover conditional and unconditional generation using both pixel-space and latent-space models. At the same NFE, F-DDIM often produces clearer structures and finer details than DDIM. In the examples shown, the higher-order solvers (DPMSolver-2/3 and UniPC-3) more often exhibit localized artifacts, particularly with few sampling steps.

A.3 Higher-order lookahead predictors

Algorithm 3 summarizes the general F-DPMSolver framework using a data prediction model. We evaluate F-DPMSolver-2, which constructs the lookahead state using the DPMSolver-2 update with cached noise predictions:

𝒙^ti=𝖮𝖣𝖤𝖲𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾𝗋𝟤⁡(𝒙ti−1,𝜺~ti−1,𝜺~ti−2),i≥2.\widehat{\bm{x}}_{t_{i}}=\mathsf{ODESolver2}\big(\bm{x}_{t_{i-1}},\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-1}},\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{i-2}}\big),\qquad i\geq 2.

The first lookahead state is constructed using (21), with 𝜺~t0=𝒙t0\widetilde{\bm{\varepsilon}}_{t_{0}}=\bm{x}_{t_{0}}. The higher-order predictor changes only the lookahead construction; each iteration still requires one new model evaluation.

Quantitative results (FID).

Tables 9 and 10 compare F-DDIM and F-DPMSolver-2 at the same NFE. F-DPMSolver-2 achieves lower FID in all reported CIFAR-10 settings and most ImageNet-512 settings. The exception is EDM2-XS at NFE =10=10, where F-DDIM achieves an FID of 4.574.57, compared with 4.904.90 for F-DPMSolver-2. These results show that a higher-order lookahead predictor can further improve sample quality in most cases. The predictor order does not determine the convergence order of the forward-value sampler. Under the lookahead accuracy condition (170), Theorem 7 in Appendix E guarantees that the sampler F-DPMSolver-2 has the first-order convergence rate of the ideal forward-value sampler.

Qualitative comparisons.

Figures 11 and 12 compare the samples generated by F-DDIM and F-DPMSolver-2. The higher-order lookahead predictor can improve visual details at small NFEs, consistent with the FID comparisons.

A.4 Larger NFE budgets and runtime comparisons

We examine F-DDIM at larger NFE budgets on ImageNet-512 using EDM2-XXL and compare runtime on ImageNet-64 using EDM2-S.

Larger NFE results.

Table 11 reports FID at NFEs 1010, 1212, 1515, and 2020. F-DDIM achieves the lowest reported FID at NFE=1010, 1212, and 1515, and matches UniPC-3 at NFE=2020. These results show that F-DDIM remains comparable to higher-order baselines over the tested range of larger NFEs.

Runtime comparison.

Table 12 compares runtime on ImageNet-64 using EDM2-S. Let T𝒜​(M)T_{\mathcal{A}}(M) denote the runtime of sampler 𝒜\mathcal{A} with MM model evaluations. We report the normalized runtime

R𝒜​(M)=10​T𝒜​(M)TDDIM​(10).R_{\mathcal{A}}(M)=10\,\frac{T_{\mathcal{A}}(M)}{T_{\mathrm{DDIM}}(10)}.

A table entry of the form M×cM\times c denotes R𝒜​(M)=M​cR_{\mathcal{A}}(M)=Mc. Thus, cc measures the average runtime per model evaluation relative to that of DDIM with NFE =10=10. F-DDIM and F-DPMSolver-2 have runtimes similar to DDIM and DPMSolver-2 at the same NFE. This supports using NFE as a practical proxy for runtime when comparing these samplers under the tested setting.

A.5 Additional samples from F-DDPM

This subsection supplements the qualitative comparisons in Section 4.2. Figures 13 and 14 show unconditional and class-conditional CIFAR-10 samples, while Figures 15 and 16 show results on ImageNet-512 and LSUN bedrooms, respectively. Within each comparison, F-DDPM and the stochastic baselines use the same NFE, initial noise, and Brownian motion. The examples illustrate that F-DDPM often produces clearer structures and finer details at small NFEs, complementing the quantitative results in Tables 3–6.

𝒙tM−𝒙tM⋆\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}^{\star} =𝑨tM​(𝒙tM−1⋆)​(𝒙tM−1−𝒙tM−1⋆)+ℰtM,1+ℰtM,2=∑m=1M∏j=m+1M𝑨tj​(ℰtm,1+ℰtm,2),\displaystyle={\bm{A}}_{t_{M}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{M-1}}^{\star})\big({\bm{x}}_{t_{M-1}}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{M-1}}^{\star}\big)+\mathcal{E}_{t_{M},1}+\mathcal{E}_{t_{M},2}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\bigg(\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},1}+\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}\bigg), (81)

where we adopt the convention that the empty product equals the identity matrix. Taking expectations and applying the triangle inequality gives the recursive bound

𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tM−𝒙tM⋆‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}^{\star}\|_{2}] ≤∑m=1M𝔼⁡[∏j=m+1M‖𝑨tj‖𝗈𝗉​‖ℰtm,1‖2]+𝔼⁡[‖∑m=1M∏j=m+1M𝑨tj​ℰtm,2‖2]\displaystyle\leq\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}\|{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\|_{\mathsf{op}}\|\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},1}\|_{2}\bigg]+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big\|\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}\Big\|_{2}\bigg] (82)

To control the product of operator norms, we first estimate a single factor. For each ii, we have

‖𝑨ti​(𝒙ti−1⋆)‖𝗈𝗉≤σtiσti−1​e−δi+αti​(1−e−2​δi)​Lxαti−1​≤(a)​1+Lx​σtiσti−1​e−δi​(e2​δi−1)​≤(b)​1+4​Lx​δi,\displaystyle\|{\bm{A}}_{t_{i}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{i-1}}^{\star})\|_{\mathsf{op}}\leq\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}+\alpha_{t_{i}}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}})\frac{L_{x}}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}\overset{\text{(a)}}{\leq}1+L_{x}\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}({\rm e}^{2\delta_{i}}-1)\overset{\text{(b)}}{\leq}1+4L_{x}\delta_{i}, (83)

where the second inequality (a) follows from σti≤σti−1\sigma_{t_{i}}\leq\sigma_{t_{i-1}} and the last inequality (b) uses e−δi​(e2​δi−1)≤4​δi{\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}({\rm e}^{2\delta_{i}}-1)\leq 4\delta_{i} for δi≤1/2\delta_{i}\leq 1/2. Consequently, the cumulative product satisfies

‖∏j=m+1M𝑨tj‖𝗈𝗉\displaystyle\Big\|\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\Big\|_{\mathsf{op}} ≤∏j=m+1M‖𝑨tj‖𝗈𝗉≤∏j=m+1M(1+4​Lx​δj)\displaystyle\leq\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}\|{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\|_{\mathsf{op}}\leq\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}(1+4L_{x}\delta_{j})
≤exp⁡(4​Lx​∑j=m+1Mδj)=O⁡(1),\displaystyle\leq\exp\big(4L_{x}\sum_{j=m+1}^{M}\delta_{j}\big)=O(1), (84)

where the last equality uses the fact that ∑j=m+1Mδj≤∑j=1Mδj=O⁡(1)\sum_{j=m+1}^{M}\delta_{j}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta_{j}=O(1). Substituting this bound into (82) yields

𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tM−𝒙tM⋆‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{M}}^{\star}\|_{2}] ≲∑m=1M𝔼⁡[‖ℰtm,1‖2]+𝔼⁡[‖∑m=1M∏j=m+1M𝑨tj​ℰtm,2‖2].\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},1}\|_{2}]+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big\|\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}\Big\|_{2}\bigg]. (85)

In the following two steps, we will bound these two contributions separately.

Step 3: Analysis of ℰtm,2\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}.

From its definition in (79b), the stochastic term ℰtm,2\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2} can be rewritten as

ℰtm,2\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2} =−22αtme−2​λtm∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤∫λtm−1λtm∫λ′λtmeλσt⁡(λ)eλ′dλd𝝎¯t⁡(λ′)\displaystyle=-2\sqrt{2}\alpha_{t_{m}}{\rm e}^{-2\lambda_{t_{m}}}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}\int_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{\lambda}\sigma_{t(\lambda)}{\rm e}^{\lambda^{\prime}}\mathrm{d}\lambda\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}
=−22αtme−2​λtm∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤∫λtm−1λtmeλ′[∫λ′λtmαt⁡(λ)dλ]d𝝎¯t⁡(λ′)\displaystyle=-2\sqrt{2}\alpha_{t_{m}}{\rm e}^{-2\lambda_{t_{m}}}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{\lambda^{\prime}}\left[\int_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}\alpha_{t(\lambda)}\mathrm{d}\lambda\right]\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}
≕∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm,\displaystyle\eqqcolon\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}, (86)

where the noise vector 𝒛¯tm\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}} depends on the Brownian motion increment over the interval [λtm−1,λtm][\lambda_{t_{m-1}},\lambda_{t_{m}}], and is defined as

𝒛¯tm≔−22αtme−2​λtm∫λtm−1λtmeλ′[∫λ′λtmαt⁡(λ)dλ]d𝝎¯t⁡(λ′).\displaystyle\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\coloneqq-2\sqrt{2}\alpha_{t_{m}}{\rm e}^{-2\lambda_{t_{m}}}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{\lambda^{\prime}}\left[\int_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}\alpha_{t(\lambda)}\mathrm{d}\lambda\right]\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}. (87)

Define the cumulative propagation matrices by

𝑷0=𝑰d,𝑷i=𝑨ti​𝑷i−1=∏j=1i𝑨tj,i≥1.\displaystyle\bm{P}_{0}=\bm{I}_{d},\qquad\bm{P}_{i}=\bm{A}_{t_{i}}\bm{P}_{i-1}=\prod_{j=1}^{i}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}},\quad i\geq 1. (88)

Note that

e−2​δi≤σtiσti−1​e−δi≤1,‖𝑨ti−𝑰d‖𝗈𝗉≤(2+4​Lx)​δi.{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{i}}\leq\frac{\sigma_{t_{i}}}{\sigma_{t_{i-1}}}{\rm e}^{-\delta_{i}}\leq 1,\qquad\|\bm{A}_{t_{i}}-\bm{I}_{d}\|_{\mathsf{op}}\leq(2+4L_{x})\delta_{i}.

Here the first inequality uses αti≥αti−1\alpha_{t_{i}}\geq\alpha_{t_{i-1}}, and the second follows from the same Jacobian bound as in (83). Writing CA=2+4​LxC_{A}=2+4L_{x}, for sufficiently small δ\delta we have

‖𝑨ti−1‖𝗈𝗉≤(1−CA​δi)−1≤exp⁡(2​CA​δi).\|\bm{A}_{t_{i}}^{-1}\|_{\mathsf{op}}\leq(1-C_{A}\delta_{i})^{-1}\leq\exp(2C_{A}\delta_{i}).

Together with (84) and ∑iδi=O⁡(1)\sum_{i}\delta_{i}=O(1), this gives a deterministic constant CC, independent of MM, such that

max0≤i≤M⁡(‖𝑷i‖𝗈𝗉+‖𝑷i−1‖𝗈𝗉)≤C.\max_{0\leq i\leq M}\bigl(\|\bm{P}_{i}\|_{\mathsf{op}}+\|\bm{P}_{i}^{-1}\|_{\mathsf{op}}\bigr)\leq C.

Then the factor in the right-hand-side of (85) becomes

∑m=1M∏j=m+1M𝑨tjℰtm,2=∑m=1M𝑨tM⋯𝑨tm+1ℰtm,2=𝑷M∑m=1M𝑷m−1ℰtm,2,\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bm{A}_{t_{M}}\cdots\bm{A}_{t_{m+1}}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}=\bm{P}_{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}, (89)

Substituting (86) into (89) yields

∑m=1M∏j=m+1M𝑨tjℰtm,2=𝑷M∑m=1M𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm.\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}=\bm{P}_{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}. (90)

To analyze this sum, define the filtration generated by the initial state and the Brownian increments up to the current log-SNR:

ℱti=σ(𝒙t0⋆,𝝎¯t⁡(λ)−𝝎¯t0:λt0≤λ≤λti).\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{t_{i}}=\sigma\Big(\bm{x}_{t_{0}}^{\star},\,\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda)}-\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t_{0}}:\lambda_{t_{0}}\leq\lambda\leq\lambda_{t_{i}}\Big). (91)

The vector 𝒛¯tm\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}} is independent of ℱtm−1\mathcal{F}_{t_{m-1}} and has zero mean. Its conditional second moment satisfies

𝔼⁡[‖𝒛¯tm‖22∣ℱtm−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t_{m-1}}] ≤8​αtm​d​e−4​λtm​∫λtm−1λtme2​λ′​[∫λ′λtmαt⁡(λ)​𝑑λ]2​d​λ′\displaystyle\leq 8\alpha_{t_{m}}d{\rm e}^{-4\lambda_{t_{m}}}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{2\lambda^{\prime}}\left[\int_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}\alpha_{t(\lambda)}\mathrm{d}\lambda\right]^{2}\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}
≤8​αtm​d​e−4​λtm​∫λtm−1λtme2​λ′​(λtm−λ′)​∫λ′λtmαt⁡(λ)2​𝑑λ​d​λ′\displaystyle\leq 8\alpha_{t_{m}}d{\rm e}^{-4\lambda_{t_{m}}}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{2\lambda^{\prime}}(\lambda_{t_{m}}-\lambda^{\prime})\int_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}\alpha_{t(\lambda)}^{2}\mathrm{d}\lambda\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}
≤8​αtm​d​e−4​λtm​∫λtm−1λtme2​λ′​δm2​αtm2​d​λ′\displaystyle\leq 8\alpha_{t_{m}}d{\rm e}^{-4\lambda_{t_{m}}}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{2\lambda^{\prime}}\delta_{m}^{2}\alpha_{t_{m}}^{2}\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}
≤8​d​δm2​αtm3​e−4​λtm​(e2​λtm−e2​λtm−1)≤16​d​δm3​αtm3​e−2​λtm=O⁡(δm3),\displaystyle\leq 8d\delta_{m}^{2}\alpha_{t_{m}}^{3}{\rm e}^{-4\lambda_{t_{m}}}({\rm e}^{2\lambda_{t_{m}}}-{\rm e}^{2\lambda_{t_{m-1}}})\leq 16d\delta_{m}^{3}\alpha_{t_{m}}^{3}{\rm e}^{-2\lambda_{t_{m}}}=O(\delta_{m}^{3}), (92)

where the second inequality follows from Jensen’s inequality, and the third uses the monotonicity αt⁡(λ)≤αtm\alpha_{t(\lambda)}\leq\alpha_{t_{m}}.

Since 𝑷m−1\bm{P}_{m}^{-1} and ∇𝝁​(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)\nabla\bm{\mu}(\bm{x}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}}) are ℱtm−1\mathcal{F}_{t_{m-1}}-measurable, and (92), the expected norm squares of the vector ∑m=1M𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}} can be computed by:

𝔼[∥∑m=1M𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm∥22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\|\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\Big\|_{2}^{2}\Big]
=∑m=1M𝔼[∥𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm∥22]\displaystyle\quad=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\big[\|\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\|_{2}^{2}\big]
+2∑n>m𝔼[⟨𝑷n−1∇𝝁(𝒙tn−1⋆,λtn−1)⊤𝒛¯tn,𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm⟩]\displaystyle\qquad+2\sum_{n>m}\mathbb{E}\big[\langle\bm{P}_{n}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{n-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{n-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{n}},\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\rangle\big]
≤C​∑m=1Mδm3=O⁡(δ2),\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{m=1}^{M}\delta_{m}^{3}=O(\delta^{2}), (93)

where the last inequality uses (92) and

𝔼[∥𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm∥22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\|\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\|_{2}^{2}\big] =𝔼[𝔼[∥𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm∥22|ℱtm−1]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}\big[\|\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\|_{2}^{2}\big|\mathcal{F}_{t_{m-1}}\big]\big]
≤C​𝔼​[𝔼⁡[‖𝒛¯tm‖22|ℱtm−1]]=O⁡(δm3),\displaystyle\leq C\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[\|\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\|_{2}^{2}\big|\mathcal{F}_{t_{m-1}}]\big]=O(\delta_{m}^{3}),

and the fact that the cross terms vanish due to the independence of 𝒛¯tn\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{n}} and ℱtn−1\mathcal{F}_{t_{n-1}}. Finally, combining (89) and (90) with Jensen’s inequality yields the required bound for the second term in (85):

𝔼​‖∑m=1M∏j=m+1M𝑨tj​ℰtm,2‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big\|\sum_{m=1}^{M}\prod_{j=m+1}^{M}{\bm{A}}_{t_{j}}\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},2}\Big\|_{2} ≲(𝔼[∥∑m=1M𝑷m−1∇𝝁(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤𝒛¯tm∥22])1/2=O(δ).\displaystyle\lesssim\Big(\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\|\sum_{m=1}^{M}\bm{P}_{m}^{-1}\nabla{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}\overline{\bm{z}}_{t_{m}}\Big\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\Big)^{1/2}=O(\delta). (94)

For later use, we also estimate 𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tm−1⋆−𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆‖22]\mathbb{E}[\|\bm{x}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}-\bm{x}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]. From (29), we have

𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆−𝒙tm−1⋆\displaystyle{\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star} =(σt⁡(λ)σtm−1​e−(λ−λtm−1)−1)​𝒙tm−1⋆\displaystyle=\Big(\frac{\sigma_{t(\lambda)}}{\sigma_{t_{m-1}}}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda-\lambda_{t_{m-1}})}-1\Big){\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}
+2αt⁡(λ)∫λtm−1λe−2​(λ−λ′)𝝁(𝒙t⁡(λ′)⋆,λ′)dλ′+2σt⁡(λ)∫λtm−1λe−(λ−λ′)d𝝎¯t⁡(λ′).\displaystyle\qquad+2\alpha_{t(\lambda)}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}^{\star},\lambda^{\prime})\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}+\sqrt{2}\sigma_{t(\lambda)}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}. (95)

Using the coefficient bound in (75) and Assumption A1, we obtain

𝔼⁡[‖𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆−𝒙tm−1⋆‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}] ≲δm2​𝔼​[‖𝒙tm−1⋆‖22]+αt⁡(λ)2​Lμ2​(∫λtm−1λe−2​(λ−λ′)​d​λ′)2\displaystyle\lesssim\delta_{m}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]+\alpha_{t(\lambda)}^{2}L_{\mu}^{2}\Big(\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}\Big)^{2}
+𝔼⁡[‖2​σt⁡(λ)​∫λtm−1λe−(λ−λ′)​d​𝝎¯t⁡(λ′)‖22].\displaystyle\qquad+\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\|\sqrt{2}\sigma_{t(\lambda)}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}\Big\|_{2}^{2}\Big]. (96)

The three terms are bounded as follows:

∫λtm−1λe−2​(λ−λ′)​d​λ′\displaystyle\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime} =12​(1−e−2​(λ−λtm−1))≤λ−λtm−1≤δm,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1-{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda-\lambda_{t_{m-1}})})\leq\lambda-\lambda_{t_{m-1}}\leq\delta_{m},
𝔼⁡[‖2​σt⁡(λ)​∫λtm−1λe−(λ−λ′)​d​𝝎¯t⁡(λ′)‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big\|\sqrt{2}\sigma_{t(\lambda)}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}\overline{\bm{\omega}}_{t(\lambda^{\prime})}\Big\|_{2}^{2}\Big] =2​d​σt⁡(λ)2​∫λtm−1λe−2​(λ−λ′)​d​λ′≤2​d​σt⁡(λ)2​δm.\displaystyle=2d\sigma_{t(\lambda)}^{2}\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda-\lambda^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}\lambda^{\prime}\leq 2d\sigma_{t(\lambda)}^{2}\delta_{m}.

Together with the moment bound 𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tm−1⋆‖22]=O⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]=O(1) from (71), we conclude

𝔼⁡[‖𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆−𝒙tm−1⋆‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}] ≲δm2+αt⁡(λ)2​Lμ2​δm+2​d​σt⁡(λ)2​δm=O⁡(δm).\displaystyle\lesssim\delta_{m}^{2}+\alpha_{t(\lambda)}^{2}L_{\mu}^{2}\delta_{m}+2d\sigma_{t(\lambda)}^{2}\delta_{m}=O(\delta_{m}). (97)
Step 4: Analysis of ℰtm,1\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},1}.

We now estimate the first term on the right-hand-side of (85). From the definition of ‖ℰtm,1‖2\|\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},1}\|_{2} in (79a), we have

𝔼⁡[‖ℰtm,1‖2]≲δm2+∫λtm−1λtme−2​(λtm−λ)​𝔼​[‖𝒙tm−1⋆−𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆‖22]​𝑑λ\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{E}_{t_{m},1}\|_{2}]\lesssim\delta_{m}^{2}+\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda_{t_{m}}-\lambda)}\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}-{\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]\mathrm{d}\lambda
+δm2​𝔼​[‖∇𝒙𝝁​(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤​𝒙tm−1⋆‖2]+δm​𝔼​[‖𝒙tm−1−𝒙tm−1⋆‖22].\displaystyle\qquad+\delta_{m}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla_{{\bm{x}}}{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}]+\delta_{m}\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}-{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]. (98)

We bound each term on the right-hand side of (98) as follows.

First, from (97), we have 𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tm−1⋆−𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆‖22]=O⁡(δm)\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}-{\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]=O(\delta_{m}). Consequently,

∫λtm−1λtme−2​(λtm−λ)​𝔼​[‖𝒙tm−1⋆−𝒙t⁡(λ)⋆‖22]​𝑑λ=O⁡(δm)​12​(1−e−2​δm)=O⁡(δm2).\displaystyle\int_{\lambda_{t_{m-1}}}^{\lambda_{t_{m}}}{\rm e}^{-2(\lambda_{t_{m}}-\lambda)}\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}-{\bm{x}}_{t(\lambda)}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]\mathrm{d}\lambda=O(\delta_{m})\frac{1}{2}(1-{\rm e}^{-2\delta_{m}})=O(\delta_{m}^{2}). (99)

Second, by Assumption A2 and the moment bound (71),

δm2​𝔼​[‖∇𝒙𝝁​(𝒙tm−1⋆,λtm−1)⊤​𝒙tm−1⋆‖2]≤Lx​δm2αtm−1​𝔼⁡[‖𝒙tm−1⋆‖22]=O⁡(δm2).\displaystyle\delta_{m}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla_{{\bm{x}}}{\bm{\mu}}({\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star},\lambda_{t_{m-1}})^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}]\leq\frac{L_{x}\delta_{m}^{2}}{\alpha_{t_{m-1}}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{m-1}}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}]}=O(\delta_{m}^{2}).
